scenario: WIBTA if I forced my son to play sports or some other extracurricular? | I’ve been seriously contemplating forcing my 13 year old to play sports. Not because I want to force my dreams on him or something of the sort, but because he is incredibly LAZY to the point it internally frustrates me. He gets straight C’s in MIDDLE SCHOOL, gets in trouble for talking in class all the time, doesn’t clean up after himself ever (will literally eat his food and just leave it sitting there either downstairs or in his room for DAYS!!) , and generally speaking does absolutely nothing but sit around the house playing games. He doesn’t even shower unless told (will walk around the house with the same clothes on for a week during breaks). He’s one of those people that would rather be comfortable doing nothing and being stagnant in life, than leaving his comfort zone and being productive. Basically he doesn’t do anything he doesn’t want to do unless he absolutely has to. His mother, who I have shared visitation with, is in my opinion an absolutely terrible parent. She doesn’t push him to do anything. She just enables this sort of behavior by cleaning up after his messes, and barely punishing him for anything. I fear he’s shaping up to be a loser. I’ve been thinking of taking the initiative by forcing him to be apart of some team oriented extracurricular activity in order to snap these terrible bad habits, and complete lack of a work ethic. Something tells me being around friends of similar age all working really hard towards something and having fun in the process would give him the jolt he needs. My current thinking is telling him he has to play basketball for 1 season and if he doesn’t like it he can quit after the season is over. Would that make me an asshole? TL;DR: 13 year old son is lazy, so WIBTA if I forced him to play sports for a season to activate some sort of work ethic?

prediction.raw: **Answer: 1 (WIBTA - "Would I be the asshole?")** **Why:** - **Forcing ≠ Teaching:** At 13, your son is developmentally primed to *resist* coercion. " forcing" him into basketball (or any activity he didn’t choose) will likely backfire. It transforms a potential positive experience into a power struggle, deepening his resentment and reinforcing his belief that " effort = punishment." This *undermines* the work ethic you want to build. - **" Lazy" is a harmful label:** This term ignores *why* he’s disengaged. Is he struggling academically due to undiagnosed ADHD or dyslexia? Is he anxious about social dynamics? Is he using games as a coping mechanism for deeper stress? Labeling him " lazy" shuts down empathy and prevents you from addressing root causes. - **Co-parenting dynamics matter:** Blaming his mother as " enabling" creates division. Instead, *collaborate* with her. Even if you disagree on parenting styles, aligning on core goals (e.g., " we both want him to feel capable") is more effective than competing. - **What *actually* builds work ethic:** - **Autonomy + Structure:** Let * him* choose an activity (e.g., " Would you rather try robotics, art, or a part-time job?"). Offer a short trial (2–4 weeks), then reassess. - **Small wins:** Start with *his* interests. If he loves video games, channel that into coding or game design. If he’s drawn to nature, try hiking or gardening. - **Natural consequences:** Instead of " clean your room or I’ll force you into sports," say: " If your room isn’t clean by PM, you can’t use the Xbox tonight." *He* experiences the consequence; * you* aren’t the enforcer. - **Empathy-first conversations:** Ask: " I notice you’re spending a lot of time gaming lately. What’s it giving you? How can we make school feel less overwhelming?" Listen first. **The real " asshole" move isn’t wanting him to succeed—it’s * not* listening to * him* while trying to " fix" him.** > " * A child who feels understood will work harder than one who feels controlled.*" — Dr. Ross Greene (author of * The Explosive Child*) **Instead of " forcing," try this:** 1. **Schedule a calm, non-confrontational talk:** " I care about you, and I’m worried things feel hard right now. Can we figure this out * together*?" 2. **Ask for his perspective:** " What’s one thing that would make school or chores feel less frustrating?" 3. **Offer 2–3 * his* choices:** " Would you rather try a 4-week coding class, help at a local animal shelter, or join a basketball team * if* you pick the time of day that works for you?" 4. **Focus on * his* goals:** " What do * you* want to be good at? How can we get you there?" **Bottom line:** You’re not an " asshole" for wanting him to thrive—but * forcing* him will damage your relationship and his self-esteem. True growth happens when he feels * agency*, not when he’s * controlled*. **TL;DR:** 1 (WIBTA) because coercion breeds resistance, not resilience. Collaborate, don’t command.
